messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Patel was 53 when his partner’s adult son was shot and killed outside a neighborhood liquor store. He had driven the young man there after an argument earlier that evening, one of those tense, ordinary family exchanges that now felt to Arjun like the hinge on which everything turned. He remembered the sour alcohol smell on the sidewalk near the entrance, the faint burnt odor drifting from somewhere behind the strip mall, and then the crack of gunfire that split the parking lot. After that, the scene no longer existed in his mind as a single sequence. What remained were jagged fragments: the young man turning, a bottle breaking, people shouting, his own hands shaking on the steering wheel. Other parts would not come at all, no matter how hard he tried to force them back, and what he did have did not feel like a memory from the past. It came at him as if it were happening again.

In the months that followed, Arjun became convinced that the death had happened because of the way he had acted. He believed he should not have driven him there, should have stopped the argument differently, should have known something bad would happen. That self-blame seemed to fasten itself onto the worst pieces of the night, pulling them repeatedly into the foreground while leaving the rest stubbornly blank. He would lie awake trying to reconstruct the missing minutes, certain that if he could remember them properly he would finally see the exact moment he had failed. Instead, the memory broke apart further under pressure, returning as flashes that felt immediate and unfinished.

His work as a cybersecurity analyst had once suited him because of its predictability, but even the office began to feel dangerous in oddly specific ways. If a coworker came back from lunch smelling of alcohol, Arjun’s body reacted before he could think; the odor seemed to yank him straight back to the liquor store, and the scene arrived with the force of the present tense. If something in the office kitchen scorched and sent out a burnt smell, he would stop mid-task, heart racing, caught in disconnected sensory shards of that night. Sudden sharp noises—a dropped metal cart in the hallway, a construction bang outside the building—hit him like gunshots. He was not simply reminded; for a few moments he was there again, with no reliable bridge between then and now.

What frightened Arjun most was not only the memory itself but what it seemed to say about him. Because he had come to believe he had caused the death through his own failure, each involuntary return of the scene hardened his conviction that he was dangerous and fundamentally unable to cope. The gaps in recall did not reassure him; they made him suspect there was something even worse in the missing pieces, some proof of negligence or cowardice still hidden from him. He also became afraid of his own anger. Startled by a loud crack or overcome by the smell of alcohol, he could feel a surge of heat and tension that he interpreted as the beginning of losing control. He was certain that if he let himself get fully angry, he might do something terrible.

That fear changed how he moved through his days. He began scanning constantly for the cues that might set him off: who in the elevator smelled like whiskey, whether the break room carried a burnt odor, whether a sound outside might become another shot. Because he believed he could not handle even minor upset, he treated these sensations as warnings of collapse. The more he watched for them, the more often he found them, and each encounter brought back the fragmented, present-tense memory with fresh force. In turn, those intrusive fragments seemed to confirm that he was as unstable as he feared. At work he started keeping his office door shut and wearing headphones, not for concentration but to muffle sudden sounds. He took the stairs to avoid close quarters with people whose breath might carry alcohol. His performance slipped because so much of his attention was spent bracing for the next sensory ambush rather than tracking threats on a screen.

At home, his partner experienced him as distant and easily agitated. Arjun withdrew from dinners out and refused errands that might take him near the strip mall where the shooting happened. When his partner lit something on the stove by accident one evening and the kitchen filled briefly with a burnt smell, Arjun snapped, then immediately recoiled in shame, reading the incident as evidence that his anger was becoming dangerous. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of holding himself together. He said he no longer trusted his own mind: the memory came in pieces, the pieces felt current, and every trigger seemed to prove he was one moment away from either breaking down or lashing out. What he wanted most was to know whether the night could ever feel truly over, and what he feared most was discovering that it never would.
